activity: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
knowledge_domain: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
fact: A delta forms where a river slows as it enters a sea or lake and drops the sediment it was carrying, building up new land.
story:
Marcus had exactly forty minutes before the trail bus left without him, and Ms. Luo had made it clear she was not waiting for stragglers. That gave him forty minutes to figure out the question on his worksheet, the one he'd been staring at since the trailhead: how does a river carve a canyon over millions of years? He was supposed to explain it to his group, and so far all he had was a blank page and a pencil that kept evaporating out of his grip because his hands were sweaty from the climb.

He caught up with Thatcher and Nadine where the trail bent around a ridge. Below them, a small stream rushed down a narrow groove in the rock, a groove so deep that Thatcher could stand in it and the water only reached his knees. "Look at this," Marcus said, crouching at the edge. "The water's all brown and gritty. It's carrying stuff." He stuck his pencil in the current and watched sand pile up against it, then swirl past. "So the river is like a saw, but a saw made of dirt it drags along."

"Sure, a saw," Thatcher said, checking his watch. "Thirty-five minutes."

They followed the stream downhill, and Marcus noticed the groove growing wider, the walls smoothed and streaked like something had rubbed them for a very long time. But the puzzling part came at the bottom, where the stream met a still green pond. Instead of just pouring in, it fanned out over a wide, low triangle of pale sand, half above the water and half below. "What is that?" Nadine said. "It looks like the stream dumped everything right there."

Marcus stood on the fan's edge. Out in the pond, the water ran clear, no grit at all. Upstream, it had been thick with sand. He scooped a handful from the fan and let it run through his fingers. "The stream slows down when it hits the pond," he said slowly, working it out as he spoke. "And when it slows, it can't hold the sand anymore, so it drops it. All that land we're standing on, the stream built it." He drew a rough sketch on his worksheet, the fan spreading wider at the bottom than the top. "It's called a delta," Nadia said, reading the label he printed under it, and Marcus nodded, because he'd seen that word somewhere before and now it had a shape and a texture and a grain of sand stuck to his palm.

"So the canyon up there and this delta down here are the same story in opposite directions," Marcus said, flipping his page over. "The river takes land away where it's fast and puts land back where it slows. Multiply that by millions of years." He scratched at an equation in the margin, river speed equals carving power or something like it, though he wasn't sure Ms. Luo would accept math that loose.

A whistle sounded from the trailhead, long and sharp. Thatcher was already jogging, and Nadine grabbed Marcus's sleeve and pulled him after her. He ran with the worksheet flapping in his hand, the delta sketch half finished, and behind him the stream went on feeding the fan, one grain at a time.

activity: to write a paragraph in a new language about plans for next year using the future tense
knowledge_domain: to write a paragraph in a new language about plans for next year using the future tense
fact: German speakers often use the present tense with a time word for future plans: "Nächstes Jahr fahre ich nach Berlin" means "Next year I am going to Berlin."
story:
Riley stared at the message from his German pen pal, Lukas, on his tablet. In language class, Ms. Lewandowski had assigned a paragraph about plans for next year, all in the future tense, and Riley had emailed Lukas to ask how he would say it. Lukas had written back a whole example sentence: "Nächstes Jahr fahre ich nach Berlin." Riley frowned. Fahre looked exactly like the present tense he had learned in September. He checked his notebook anyway, and there it was, ich fahre, I am going, present tense. His pen pal had made a mistake, Riley was sure of it, and correcting Lukas would make him look like he actually understood German.

The classroom smelled like the marker Ms. Lewandowski had just used on the board, and outside the window the oak trees were still lush and green, refusing to admit it was November. Philip leaned over from the next desk. "Just tell him he used the wrong tense. It's one word, change it, done."

But something bothered Riley. Lukas wrote German every single day. Why would he mess up something that basic? Riley flipped through the workbook to the page of letters from German kids that Ms. Lewandowski had photocopied. He found a letter from a girl named Anna. "Morgen gehe ich ins Kino," she had written. Tomorrow I go to the movies. Present tense again, but with a time word. Then another: "Im Sommer fahre ich nach Spanien." In the summer I go to Spain. Riley sat up so fast his chair squeaked.

He raised his hand. "Ms. Lewandowski, can I check something?" He read Lukas's sentence out loud. "Nächstes Jahr fahre ich nach Berlin. That's present tense, but he means next year. Did he mess up, or is that how it works?"

She smiled and said, "Nächstes Jahr fahre ich nach Berlin means next year I am going to Berlin." That was all she said, and Riley heard it: German speakers used the present tense with a time word for future plans. Lukas hadn't made a mistake at all. Riley had almost corrected a native speaker on his own language.

"Wait," said Zaid from across the room, "so we don't need the future tense for the assignment?"

"You still practice it," Ms. Lewandowski said. "But your paragraph will sound natural either way."

Riley wrote his paragraph twice, once with the future tense and once with the present tense plus a time word, like Nächstes Jahr fahre ich nach Kanada. He decided the second version was his real one. He would send it to Lukas first, before he handed it in, because Lukas had earned the right to check Riley's work after Riley had doubted his. At home that night, Riley typed the message, hit send, and watched the little whoosh animation emit from the mailbox icon on his screen.

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: A fallen power line can still carry deadly electricity even when it is not sparking, so it should be treated as live, kept well away from, and reported.
story:
The lights went out just as William sat down to dinner, and the whole house dropped into a blue darkness that smelled of the half-cooked pasta still on the stove. He found his phone by its glow and texted Quinn: did you lose power too? While he waited for the answer, he kept thinking about the walk home, about the wire lying across the sidewalk three streets over, black and quiet, not doing anything at all.

"Stay off the stove," his mom called from the hallway, her voice mediating between his worry and the darkness like she could talk the evening back to normal. "The gas is still on, but I don't want you bumping around blind."

Quinn texted back fast. YES. and then, is it because of the wire? William stared at the words. That was the thing that had spooked him most about it. The wire wasn't sparking. It just lay there across the concrete like a garden hose somebody dropped, and his first instinct had been to step over it and keep going, because it looked dead. Quinn had grabbed his sleeve. "Don't," Quinn had said. "A fallen line can still be live even when it's not sparking. You treat it like it's on. You keep away and you report it." William had argued for about four seconds, pointing out that it wasn't doing anything, and then the words had landed properly and he'd stepped back off the sidewalk so fast he'd nearly tripped.

They had turned around, both of them, and cut through the Hendersons' yard, which Quinn insisted was porous enough to count as a public shortcut even though the fence said otherwise. Mr. Oliveira had been out front sweeping storm twigs off his steps, and he'd listened without interrupting, which somehow made William feel more believed, not less. "Good call," Mr. Oliveira had said, phone already in his hand. "I'll report it now. You two go straight home." He'd called it in right there in front of them, reading the cross streets off his fingers.

Now, sitting on the kitchen floor with his phone light pointed at the ceiling, William turned the whole thing over in his mind. If he had stepped over that wire, he'd probably be fine. Probably. He thought about how the quiet ones, the ones that looked harmless, were the dangerous ones, and how that felt true about other things too. He'd spent half of last year assuming Asha was stuck-up because she ate lunch alone, and then a group project had proven him completely wrong, and he'd had to admit to himself that he'd been working off a stereotype, a lazy picture in his head instead of the actual person. The wire and Asha weren't the same, exactly. But both times the surface had told him a lie.

His phone buzzed. Mr. Oliveira, of all people: crews are on your street, power by 8 if it goes right. William read it twice, then called up the stairs, "Mom! Mr. Oliveira says the crews are here!" He stood, phone light bobbing, and crossed to the dark window. At the corner, a truck's amber beacon swept slow circles across the wet pavement, over and over.

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Streaming video uses far more mobile data than sending text messages, so watching videos away from Wi-Fi can use up a data plan quickly.
story:
The phone was warm in Isabelle's pocket, two days old, and already the best thing she owned. On the bus Monday morning she sat beside Karen and pulled it out. "My mom permits me one hour a day," she said, "if my homework's done."

"Then you have to show me that video app," Karen said. "Breanna found one with skateboarding dogs. Watch, it's hilarious."

Isabelle watched. Then she watched another, and another, laughing until the bus turned into the school loop. She did the same on the ride home, and every ride after that. It felt like the phone had been waiting all her life for exactly this.

On Sunday night her mother knocked on her door and held out her hand. "You used it all up," she said quietly. "The whole month's data. In one week."

Isabelle stared at the screen. A little message sat at the top: no data remaining. She thought of her father last spring, holding his own phone, sighing at a bill he wouldn't let her see. She hadn't understood it then. Now something clicked into place, like a rule she'd been staring at without seeing. The videos were the problem. Streaming video used far more mobile data than sending text messages did, so watching them away from Wi-Fi could drain a whole plan in days. That had to be it. She sent Karen a text, counted the seconds, checked the data meter on her phone. Nothing moved, or nothing she could see. One text weighed almost nothing next to a video.

Monday morning she found Karen in their usual seat. "I figured out what happened," she said. "The dog videos. They eat data like crazy. Texting barely touches it."

Karen's face fell, and Isabelle caught what she wasn't saying out loud: the bus rides were about to get boring, and maybe Karen thought she'd done something wrong.

"We can still text each other the links," Isabelle said. "I'll watch them at home, on Wi-Fi, and tell you the best parts. Deal?"

Karen grinned. "Deal. You're a way better protagonist than those dog videos anyway."

"Rebellious skateboard dogs," Isabelle said, typing. "Coming to a Wi-Fi connection near you."

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: Tropical rainforests lie near the equator, where strong sunlight heats moist air that rises, cools and forms clouds, often bringing heavy afternoon rain.
story:
The departures board at Gate 14 flickered, and Evelyn's science project flickered with it. Her connecting flight to Phoenix, where she was supposed to collect desert data, was delayed by weather, and her rainfall and temperature graphs were due on Monday. She sat on the cold floor beside her suitcase and stared at the two nearly empty pages in her notebook.

"Rough luck," said Shreya, plopping down next to her with a bag of pretzels. Jenson leaned over Evelyn's shoulder from the row of chairs behind them.

"You could still do the rainforest half," he said. "Mr. Xu's cousin flew in from the Amazon last night. She's waiting at Gate 12 right now, and she's got like a thousand photos on her phone."

Evelyn remembered a lesson from October, when Mr. Xu had shown the class a rainfall graph shaped like a jagged mountain range. He had asked them to speculate about why the rainforest bars climbed so high every single month, and Evelyn had guessed wrong, saying it must be hurricanes. He'd smiled and said to look closer. She still didn't know what she'd missed.

At Gate 12, a woman with mud on her boots scrolled through her photos willingly. Evelyn copied dates and times into her notebook while Shreya wrote down what the sky looked like in each picture. That's when the pattern showed up. Every morning shot had blue sky. Every single afternoon shot had black clouds and rain hammering down, the kind Jenson called "aggressive weather."

"That's strange," Evelyn said. "My desert graph from the textbook is the opposite. Almost no rain all year, hot days, cold nights. But the rainforest gets soaked every afternoon. Same strong sun near the equator, so why the difference?" She tapped her pencil. "The desert air is dry, so nothing happens. The rainforest air must be full of moisture. The sun heats it, the moist air rises, cools, forms clouds, and then it pours."

"So the whole rainforest cycle repeats every day?" Shreya asked.

"Near the equator, yes," Evelyn said, sketching a little diagram of rising air and a cloud with fat raindrops. She drew a second diagram of flat desert heat, sun beating on sand with no clouds to answer it.

"But you still need real numbers for your graph," Jenson said. "You can't turn photos into bars."

Evelyn frowned at her notebook, then pulled out her phone and found the airport's weather app, which listed hourly conditions for Manaus, Brazil, sitting right on the equator. Hour after hour of rainfall percentages stacked up like stairs, climbing through the afternoon. She copied the pattern onto graph paper, filling in the rainforest bars while the real rain outside tapped the terminal glass in the same rhythm.

"Desert in the morning," she said, holding up the finished graph, "rainforest by three o'clock."

"Boarding now for Phoenix," the gate agent announced, and Evelyn zipped her notebook into her bag and ran.

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: iPhones and Android phones let you choose, app by app, whether an app may use your location always, only while you are using it, or never.
story:
Emma logged into the computer lab's shared tablet and found a message waiting in the game's chat: "Nice hoodie today. Red suits you." She had not posted any photo. She had not mentioned the hoodie to anyone in the game.

She put the tablet down and looked across the lab. Rafaelle was two seats over, headphones on, thumbs flying through the same game, Treasure Run. Jean leaned over Rafaelle's shoulder, pointing at the screen.

"You got a weird message too?" Emma asked Rafaelle.

Rafaelle pulled one headphone off. "Some account called RunnerNine keeps messaging me. Says he knows what street I live on."

Jean straightened up. "That's creepy."

Emma scrolled her own chat again. RunnerNine had commented on her lunch yesterday. Sandwich, orange, the corner table. She had eaten alone in the gym hallway, nowhere near anyone she knew. Nobody could have seen her there unless they had been in the hallway, and the hallway had been empty.

"Show me your phone," she said to Rafaelle.

"Why?"

"Just show me."

Rafaelle handed it over, the elastic band of his case stretched loose from being yanked on and off. Emma went into settings, found the app list, and tapped Treasure Run. The screen said Location: Always. She checked her own phone. Always. Jean's. Always. Three phones, three copies of the same setting.

"There's a choice here," Emma said. "Always, only while using the app, or never. iPhones and Androids both let you pick, app by app. Every single app, you get to decide."

"So change it," Jean said. "Easy."

Emma changed hers to Never and waited. She opened the game, walked her character to the fountain where RunnerNine always showed up, and typed nothing. For two days RunnerNine had found her there every afternoon. Today the account appeared, asked where she was, and asked again. Then it went quiet.

Rafaelle had already changed his setting, but Jean was still typing, jaw set. The school talent show audition was Thursday, and RunnerNine had promised to "post her audition song everywhere." Jean wanted the song kept secret until the audition; that was the whole plan, a surprise entrance nobody could copy.

"Change it," Emma said.

"He already has my street."

"He has your street. He doesn't have Thursday."

Jean's thumbs hovered. Then she flipped the setting to Never and shut the game.

After school, Emma walked the long way home, past the gym hallway, and stopped at the corner table. She looked around slowly. Nobody. Only the camera above the door, humming faintly as its motor began to accelerate, turning to follow the empty hall.

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: 1 is not a prime number; mathematicians exclude it so that every whole number has only one way to be written as a product of primes.
story:
Quinn had typed her whole program twice already, and it still printed "prime" when she typed 1 into the box. She sat back on the picnic bench outside the coding cabin and glared at the laptop screen as though it were a classmate who had lied to her.

"You're stuck too?" Amara asked, sliding onto the bench with her own laptop balanced on one arm. Around them the camp buzzed with its conventional summer noises, canoes knocking against the dock, someone's radio, kids yelling on the far field. Inside the cabin, Mr. Dela Cruz was moving between tables, but Quinn wanted to solve this one herself before asking him.

"It says 1 is prime," Quinn said. "Try my program. Type a 1." Amara typed it, and the screen answered "prime" in cheerful white letters. Quinn chewed her thumbnail. She knew the usual rule a number is prime if nothing divides it except itself and 1, and by that rule, 1 almost seemed to qualify. But something about it bothered her, the way a splinter bothers you before you can see it.

"Try 6," she said suddenly. Amara typed it: not prime. "Try 8." Not prime. "Try 12." Not prime. Quinn was hunting for the pattern, testing small numbers the way you tap a wall to find the hollow spot. "Break them down," she murmured, and on paper she factored each one: 6 was 2 times 3, 8 was 2 times 2 times 2, 12 was 2 times 2 times 3. Every one came apart into primes, and into only one arrangement of primes, no matter how she shuffled the multiplication. That felt like a rule underneath everything, invisible until you wrote it out. Then she wrote the number 1 on the paper and circled it, and stopped.

"Wait," she said. "If 1 counted as prime, you could multiply any answer by 1 as many times as you liked. Six could be 2 times 3, or 2 times 3 times 1, or 2 times 3 times 1 times 1, forever." Amara frowned at the paper. "So it wouldn't be one way anymore." "Exactly. That's the whole point. Mathematicians leave 1 out so every whole number has only one way to be written as a product of primes." The plague of extra 1s, multiplying like mosquitoes, made her laugh out loud.

Quinn added one line to the program, an if statement that sent the number 1 straight to "not prime" before anything else ran. She ran it, typed 1, and watched the screen print the right answer at last. Amara bumped her shoulder. "Show Mr. Dela Cruz before lunch." Quinn closed the laptop, hugged it to her chest for a second like something she would cherish, and stood up. "Race you to the cabin."

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: Some element symbols come from Latin names, such as Fe for iron, from the Latin word ferrum.
story:
Muhammad spread the periodic table across the kitchen table, weighting one corner with the salt shaker and the other with a mug. Tomorrow's quiz would ask him to find the number of protons in any element, and Ms. Singh had made it sound easy: the atomic number told you the protons. Easy for her. She wrote the thing for a living.

His little sister's sensor-like talent for detecting snacks meant she appeared at his elbow within thirty seconds, but even she lost interest in a wall of tiny boxes and drifted away. Muhammad ran his pencil down the columns. Hydrogen, one proton. Helium, two. Carbon, six. That part worked. Then he tried to look up iron, because iron was a real thing, the thing in his blood and in the gate outside, and he hunted for a big letter I. He found iodine instead, sitting there with its I like it owned the place. That could irritate a person. Somewhere in the middle of the table, where iron should have been, sat a box labeled Fe.

He checked his printout twice, wondering if the school had handed out a negligent copy, one with a typo nobody had bothered to fix. Fe. He said it out loud. "Eff-ee." His mother, slicing onions at the counter, said, "In Urdu we say faulad, but your grandmother calls it loha." Neither word started with F either.

Muhammad texted Pierce, who was supposedly studying the same quiz. Pierce replied with a shrugging emoji and the message "maybe iron is special." That was Pierce's answer to most things. Muhammad narrowed it down the only way he could: he flipped the sheet over, found the tiny footnote crammed at the bottom, and read it. Some element symbols came from Latin names. Fe for iron came from the Latin word ferrum. He read it again. Then he counted the box. Iron, twenty-six. Twenty-six protons, sitting in every nail in the garage.

He tested the idea on the rest of the table, hunting other symbols that didn't match their English names. Sodium was Na. Potassium was K. The old Romans, it turned out, had gotten to the naming first, and nobody had bothered to change the labels, the way nobody in his family bothered to fix the drawer that only opened if you lifted it slightly.

Hazel called at eight, panicking about the quiz. "I can't find an I for iron anywhere," she said. "The table's broken."

"It's not broken," Muhammad said. "Fe. Ferrum. It's Latin."

A long pause. Then: "You're making that up."

"Twenty-six protons," he said, and folded the sheet along its worn crease.

activity: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why
knowledge_domain: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why
fact: A share of stock is a small piece of ownership in a company, so a stockholder owns part of the business and shares in its gains or losses.
story:
Layla stood outside Sole City at the mall, holding the envelope her grandfather had given her that morning. Inside was a crisp certificate saying she owned one share of Vector Footwear. One share. She had read it four times on the bus, and the more she read it, the more one question clawed at her: did owning part of a sneaker company mean she got sneakers?

Apollo and Graydon were already inside, hovering over a wall of display shoes like they might colonize the whole aisle if the cashier looked away. Layla held up the certificate.

"Check this out. My grandpa gave me a piece of Vector."

Graydon leaned in. "A piece? Like a coupon?"

"No. It says a share of stock is a small piece of ownership in the company. So I own part of the business."

Apollo grabbed a lime-green high-top from the rack. "Then these are, like, partly yours. Take them to the register and say you're an owner."

Layla's heart actually jumped. It sounded too easy, but she couldn't see why it wouldn't work. Owning part of a business should mean something you could hold. She carried the shoe to the counter, where a bored cashier waited, and slid the certificate across.

"I own a share of this company," she said. "So do I get these free, or at least a discount?"

The cashier squinted at the certificate, then at her. "One share is one tiny sliver, hon. You share in the gains or losses, not the merchandise. That'll be eighty-four ninety-nine."

Her face went hot. She thanked him and walked back to the boys, setting the shoe down carefully, as if it might blame her.

"So it's not free shoes," she said slowly. "It's the money the company makes. If the business does well, my piece is worth more. If it does badly, my piece is worth less. That's what sharing in gains and losses means."

"Which is why my mom bought a bond instead," Graydon said. "She says a bond is just lending the company money, and they pay her back with interest. No ownership, no sharing anything."

Layla turned that over. "Then the bond is safer, right? The company owes her either way. But with stock, whether I gain or lose depends on the whole business doing well or badly. Stock has to be riskier." She paused. "Unless she picks some random company that goes broke. Then nobody gets paid."

Apollo pointed at the shoe wall. "So your verdict is keep the certificate and pay for the sneakers?"

"My verdict is that I own exactly one sliver of this company, and eighty-four ninety-nine is staying in my pocket today." She tucked the certificate back into the envelope, smoothed the flap shut, and pressed it flat against her chest as she headed for the exit.

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: Crying when a parent leaves is called separation anxiety; it is a normal stage of development that commonly begins in the second half of a baby's first year.
story:
Sebastian had agreed to watch the neighbor's baby mostly because his cousin owed the neighbor a favor and his cousin was, according to his aunt, "completely unreliable." That was how Sebastian ended up in his cousin's living room at seven o'clock on a Friday, holding a ten-month-old named Robby while the parents waved goodbye. Robby waved back with one small hand, smiled, and then, the instant the door clicked shut, turned his face into Sebastian's shoulder and screamed like a siren.

The parents had said they would be back by nine. Sebastian checked the clock: two hours. Robby screamed through the first ten minutes of it, his whole body rigid, his fists knotted in Sebastian's shirt. Sebastian tried rocking, which did nothing. He tried bouncing, which made it worse. He could feel the heat of the kid's face through his sleeve, and his arm was starting to ache from the weight.

He pulled out his phone with his free hand and texted Laila, whose little brother had been a baby only last year. "Neighbor's baby screams when parents leave. How long does this last? They're back at 9." While he waited, he reasoned it out loud, quietly, over the howling. Robby had smiled at the door before it closed. He wasn't hurt, wasn't hungry; the parents had fed him right in front of Sebastian. The crying had started exactly when the parents disappeared. So the cause wasn't something Sebastian could see, like a wet diaper or a fever. It was something invisible, a rule in the kid's head about who should be there and who shouldn't.

Laila texted back a photo of a page from her mom's baby book, complete with its citation and publisher, and beneath it: "It's called separation anxiety. My mom says it's a normal stage, starts in the second half of the first year. It fades fast if you distract them."

Sebastian read it twice. A normal stage, not an emergency. That changed things. He dismissed his plan of calling the parents, set the phone down, and carried Robby to the kitchen, where the dishwasher was making its low, rumbling whoosh. Robby hiccupped, lifted his head, and stared at it. Sebastian opened the cabinet above it so the door swung with a soft creak, then shut it, then opened it again, like a game. Robby's next cry came out crooked, almost curious. Sebastian grabbed a plastic measuring cup from the counter and banged it gently on the cabinet. Robby grabbed for it with both hands, tears still shining on his cheeks, and banged it himself, harder, delighted.

By eight thirty they were on the floor with a wooden spoon and a pot, and Robby was laughing so hard he fell over sideways. When the parents' car pulled into the driveway, Robby stood up at the window, banging the spoon against the glass, and shouted one wet, triumphant syllable at the headlights.

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: Line dances, in which a group repeats the same set of steps facing the same direction, let people dance together without needing a partner.
story:
Lucas stood at the edge of the gym with his phone buzzing in his pocket, and he already knew who it was. The family group chat had been going since four o'clock. His mom had sent a photo of his collared shirt with the caption "the one?" His grandfather had replied with twelve thumbs-up. His aunt had asked what time the dance ended, which nobody could clarify, since nobody in the chat actually knew.

Across the gym, Aditya and Trenton were leaning against the bleachers, holding cups of punch and pretending not to watch the dance floor. Lucas joined them. The floor was full near the stage and empty everywhere else, like a magnet was pulling everybody to one corner.

"Notice anything?" Trenton said. "Half the grade is over there and nobody has a partner. Emma's dancing next to people she doesn't even talk to."

Lucas watched. The song changed, and the whole crowd turned to face the same direction, all at once, like a flock of birds. Then they stepped to the side, clapped, and stepped back. A few kids lagged a beat behind, and nobody cared. It clicked.

"It's a line dance," Aditya said, following his gaze. "Everybody repeats the same set of steps, facing the same direction, the whole time. No partner needed."

"So you just learn the steps and you're in?" Lucas asked.

"That's the entire system," Aditya said.

Lucas's phone buzzed again. His dad, in the chat: "Any luck?" Then his grandmother: "Don't just stand there, go dance." Then a photo of the family cat, apparently for moral support. He typed back "going in" and slid the phone into his pocket. His obligation to the chat could wait ninety seconds.

The steps were a grapevine to the right, a clap, a grapevine back, then a diagonal step forward with a little hitch, like a shovel stuck in the ground. Lucas missed the first clap entirely, hit the second one late, and then his feet found the count on their own. The kid beside him, some seventh grader he'd never met, gave him a nod without breaking stride. Nobody asked anybody anything. Everybody just faced the same way and did the thing.

By the third song Lucas had stopped counting. Trenton had joined on his left, arms doing something that was legally questionable but effective. Aditya stayed by the punch, filming, which Lucas decided to forgive later.

At the door, Mr. Fraser, who was supervising the exit, held up his own phone. "Your family chat is lighting up my view of the room, kid. Your grandmother wants video."

"She can have four seconds," Lucas said, and filmed the line, all of them stepping right, clapping, and turning together.

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: Masaccio's Holy Trinity fresco in Florence, painted around 1427, is one of the earliest paintings built on a single vanishing point.
story:
Katherine pressed her pencil so hard against the paper that the street she was drawing looked like it had been sketched by an angry woodpecker. The buildings leaned toward each other like tired old men, and the road refused to go anywhere at all.

"You're supposed to be drawing a street," said Tina, leaning over her shoulder with a granola bar in one hand. "That looks like a pile of crackers."

"Thank you for your art review." Katherine erased for the tenth time. The art contest deadline was Friday, and the rules excluded anything traced or printed, so she could not cheat her way out of this one. Ms. Kang's class had a print of Masaccio's Holy Trinity fresco, painted around 1427 in Florence, and Ms. Kang had lent it to Katherine over the weekend. "Earliest single vanishing point in town," she had said with a wink, whatever that meant.

Priya arrived with the print rolled under her arm like a scroll from a very dusty king. They spread it on the kitchen table, next to the orange juice and Katherine's failed streets. Priya squinted at it. "Okay, so the ceiling lines," she said, and touched the printed vaulting with one finger. "They slant."

Katherine grabbed a ruler from the junk drawer. "Then let's see where they slant to." She laid the ruler along one ceiling edge, then another, then a floor edge. Tina held a pretzel stick along a different line for scale, ate it, and held another. The lines kept crossing in one spot, again and again, right in the middle of the fresco behind the figures.

"That's the vanishing point," Katherine said. "One point. Everything aims at it." She flipped her drawing paper over to a clean side and made a small dot near the top, like a lone freckle. From the dot she drew lines fanning outward, then set her ruler between them and drew the edges of a road that actually ran away from her, shrinking toward the dot like it was scared of it.

"It looks real," Priya said, sounding genuinely annoyed about it.

"The buildings next," Katherine said, her pencil moving fast now. She left gaps for windows so the whole street would not be one solid gray block, because a street with nothing alive in it was like a pond with no ecosystem, technically a street but basically a ghost town.

"Careful, though," Tina said, tapping the dot. "You built your whole world on one little pencil freckle. It's extremely vulnerable."

Katherine grinned and pressed a finger over the dot. "Then I defend it with my life."

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: Results from a large sample are generally more reliable than results from a few people, because chance differences between individuals tend to even out in larger groups.
story:
Madison stood in aisle three of Ridgeline Pharmacy with a nose like a blocked drain and a decision to make. In front of her, a pyramid of tissue boxes rose beside a bright green display of Cold-Be-Gone throat spray. The sign said "Users report feeling better fast." Her friend Manreet had texted her an hour ago: GET THE SPRAY. My cousin used it and was totally fine in two days. Manreet had also called the spray radical, though Manreet called most things radical, including a cafeteria burrito on Tuesday.

Madison picked up a bottle and turned it over. On the back, in print small enough to hide from a hawk, it said "Based on a survey of users." It did not say how many users. One could be a lot of users, technically, if the one was Manreet's cousin. She put the bottle back and accidentally elbowed the tissue pyramid, which began to collapse in slow motion, like a building deciding against itself. She caught three boxes and demoted the rest to a shorter, more honest pyramid.

Ms. Brennan, the pharmacist, appeared around the corner with the calm expression of someone who had witnessed many tissue disasters. "Can I help you find something?"

"The spray," Madison said. "The sign says users report feeling better fast. How many users?"

"Seventeen," said Ms. Brennan, and refilled a basket of cough drops without further comment.

Seventeen. Madison stood there doing arithmetic in her head. In her science class, they had once surveyed the whole grade, two hundred kids, about the cafeteria snacks, and the results were nothing like what three friends had told her beforehand. Three friends had said everybody loved the pizza dippers. Two hundred kids said no such thing. She had thought about that for a week. With only seventeen people, a couple of lucky folks who were getting better anyway could make the whole survey glow. With two hundred, the lucky ones got swallowed up in the crowd and the truth showed through. Seventeen didn't scare her. Seventeen barely qualified as a crowd.

She did a quick test of her own, since she was already standing there. For ten minutes she loitered near the display, pretending to study a bottle of fish oil capsules whose label claimed the salmon were raised in pristine northern estuaries. She counted customers. Nine people walked past the spray. One man bought it, along with cigarettes and a lottery ticket, which told her something about his general luck. One out of ten, and she was guessing that one was not going to phone in a review either way.

Manreet arrived at four o'clock, drawn by the texts, and grabbed two bottles immediately. "It's radical," she said. "My cousin."

"Your cousin is one person," said Madison. "Seventeen is seventeen people. Two hundred is two hundred people. Order matters."

"That's the most boring sentence anyone has ever said in a pharmacy."

Madison put the spray back, bought the tissues she had already half demolished, and went home. She drank water, slept eleven hours, and complained at a professional level. Two days later her cold was gone. She texted Manreet: feeling better fast, no spray. Manreet texted back: my cousin says that's because of the spray's energy field. Madison read it twice, set the phone face down on her desk, and reached for another tissue.

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
knowledge_domain: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
fact: Repeating a measurement several times and taking the average gives a more reliable result than a single try.
story:
Arthur had wanted the window seat in the science lab all year, and today it finally happened, which was how he ended up trying to measure the speed of a rolling ball while Alessio kept tapping the glass to wave at pigeons. Ms. Farah-Ali had set the ramp at the end of the long bench and told them to time the ball over two metres, then plot distance against time on graph paper. Arthur marked the start line and the finish line with pencil and waited for Alessio to stop distracting birds.

"You release, I time," Alessio said, holding the stopwatch like it might bite him. The ball rolled, he clicked, and they wrote down 1.9 seconds. Arthur did the division in the margin, speed equals distance divided by time, a formula he actually liked because it always gave an answer. Two metres in 1.9 seconds. He started drawing his graph, plotting the point neatly.

The second try gave 2.0 seconds. The third gave 1.1 seconds, which was so different that Arthur stopped drawing. He checked the lines on the bench, wondering if the ball had somehow evaded the finish line, or if Alessio had clicked late. Alessio insisted he hadn't. "Do it again," Arthur said, and they did it twice more: 1.9, then 2.0. Five numbers now, four of them clustered together and one sitting far away like a stranger.

Arthur stared at the page. Last term, in the bridge-building contest, he had used a single measurement for the weight his model could hold, and it had snapped on the second test at the science fair while the judge watched. He had blamed the glue. Now he wasn't so sure. He crossed out nothing, but he circled the four close numbers and added them up, then divided by four. "Repeating it and taking the average," he said slowly, "gives a more reliable result than one try." He felt odd saying it out loud, like admitting something about himself as well as the ball. He averaged all five too, and saw how the odd one dragged the answer away from where the ball really seemed to live.

Ms. Farah-Ali walked past and looked at his circled numbers. "Which one are you going with?" she asked. Arthur pointed at the four-number average and explained about the outlier, possibly a late click, possibly something nobody would ever know. She nodded once and moved on, indifferent to the drama it had cost him, which somehow made him feel better.

Then Tucker leaned over from the next bench, holding his own sheet with a single triumphant time on it and a beautiful graph already drawn. "One try, done," he said. "Fastest in the room, probably." Arthur looked at Tucker's number, then at his own five messy readings, and started to smile without quite meaning to, because Tucker's one reading was 0.8 seconds, and there was no way on that ramp in the world.

activity: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia
knowledge_domain: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia
fact: Mawsynram, in India's Meghalaya state, is often called the wettest place on Earth, averaging nearly 12 meters of rain a year.
story:
Brody had forty minutes before the bus came, and one assignment standing between him and Friday: explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia. He spread his notes across the library table and stared at the blank page. Ms. Dlamini, the librarian, had already walked past twice, and he could tell from her raised eyebrows that she noticed he had written exactly one word, "rain," and then stopped.

"You look like a boy excavating his own desk," Kim said, dropping into the chair beside him with a stack of books about weather.

"I don't get how it works," Brody said. "I can't see wind moving a whole ocean of air. There's no picture of it happening. Just diagrams with arrows."

Kim flipped open one of her books. "Then stop trying to see it and look for proof it happened." She turned the book around. A photo showed a village half buried in green hills, water streaming off the slopes.

Brody leaned in. The caption said Mawsynram, in India's Meghalaya state, is often called the wettest place on Earth, averaging nearly 12 meters of rain a year. He read it twice. "Twelve meters. That's like stacking six of me on top of each other, and it all falls in one year."

"That's not normal rain," Kim said. "That's a monster."

"So something invisible is dumping an ocean on that town every single summer," Brody said slowly. He pulled the diagram toward him, the one with the big arrows he'd been ignoring. If that much water came off the sea again and again, the arrows had to mean the wind was dragging moisture from the ocean toward the land. He grabbed a pencil and drew clouds riding the arrow lines like train cars on a track. Rice paddies needed flooding, so if the monsoon came late or weak, the whole harvest could fail. "It's not just weather," he said. "It's dinner for millions of people. That's why it matters."

Leandre appeared at the table, back from the printer. "Ms. Dlamini says we have ten minutes before she kicks us out for the book club."

Brody kept writing. His hand cramped and his first two sentences still sounded like a textbook that had swallowed a dictionary, but the middle part worked: the invisible wind, the sea, the rice. "My brain feels like one neuron firing in the dark," he muttered.

"One's enough to start with," Kim said, and slid the pencil back toward him.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: Philosopher Karl Popper argued, in a book first published in 1934, that an idea is scientific only if some possible observation could prove it wrong.
story:
Declan's project sat on the kitchen table in three shoeboxes: two sprouting bean plants and one that had not sprouted at all. The problem was that he had no idea why the third one had failed, and the science fair was in two days. His dad had watered them all the same amount, the window light was the same, and the soil came from the same bag. Declan pulled out his notebook and wrote, "Hypothesis: the seeds in box three were dead before I planted them." It was a guess, but at least it was a guess about something he could check.

He texted Yazan because Yazan's older sister had won the fair last year. Half an hour later Yazan replied with a photo of a page from a library book, and under it a message: "it says a guy named Karl Popper argued, in a book first published in 1934, that an idea is scientific only if some possible observation could prove it wrong. so ur judge might ask u what would show ur idea was false." Declan read it twice. He had been thinking about how to prove his idea was right. He had not once thought about how to prove it was wrong.

He wrote back, "if I plant 5 more seeds from the same packet and they all sprout, my hypothesis is wrong, because then the seeds aren't dead." Yazan sent back a thumbs-up and the words "that's ur Popper move." Declan planted five seeds from the packet in fresh soil, labeled the cup, and set it beside the window. Then he thought of something else and planted five more from a different packet as a comparison. While he worked, his friend Macey arrived to borrow his bike pump and stopped at the table.

"Which one's your project?" she asked.

"All of it. The dead-seed idea is my hypothesis. It's a testable guess, so an experiment can support it or knock it down."

"That's grim," Macey said. "You sound pessimistic about your own project."

Declan shook his head. "Wanting to knock it down isn't pessimistic. It's the whole point." He tapped the notebook. "If nothing could ever prove me wrong, then I'm just saying stuff, not doing science."

The next morning, two green hooks had broken the soil in the new cup from the original packet. Declan stared at them, crossed out his hypothesis in the notebook, and wrote a new one about overwatering. He carried the cup to the sink to pour off the extra water.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: Children and teenagers should not take aspirin during flu or chickenpox, because it is linked to Reye's syndrome, a rare but serious illness affecting the liver and brain.
story:
Xavier had been sent to his grandmother's house to recover from the flu, with strict instructions to rest, drink fluids, and stay in the spare room where the afternoon light came through lace curtains. His head ached and his temperature had climbed again by the third day, so he shuffled to the bathroom cabinet in his socks, hunting for something to bring it down.

The cabinet held cough drops, a half-empty bottle of cold syrup, and a familiar orange bottle labeled aspirin. He reached for it automatically, then paused. His mother had said something once, back when he had chickenpox in fifth grade, something about not taking aspirin. He couldn't remember what, only that she had taken the bottle away from him with a look he'd never seen before. Now he turned the aspirin bottle in his hand, reading the small print, and found a warning addressed to exactly his situation: children and teenagers with flu or chickenpox should not use this product. It didn't say why.

He brought the bottle downstairs, where his grandfather was negotiating with a crossword puzzle and a pencil he refused to admit was too short. "Grandpa, why can't kids with the flu take aspirin?" Xavier asked, setting the bottle on the table. His grandfather lowered the puzzle.

"Your grandmother could tell you better, but the short answer is Reye's syndrome," he said. "Rare, but serious. Hits the liver and the brain." He tapped the bottle. "That's why it's off-limits until you're grown. There's acetaminophen in the kitchen cabinet, second shelf. That one's fine for you."

Xavier found the right bottle, checked its label twice, and took the correct dose with a glass of water. Later, sprawled on the spare room bed, he texted Kaley, who had been sending him homework updates all week. Her reply came as a longer message, almost a letter: "Hussein had the flu last month and his mom cleared all the aspirin out of their bathroom before he even got home from school. He asked me today if you were contagious and if I'd caught it, so he's clearly back to normal. Also Ms. Clarke says the history essay can wait until you're better, so don't stress. Drink something. Kaley."

He read it twice, then a third time, because something was nagging at him. Hussein's mom had removed the aspirin before Hussein even walked in the door. That was consistent with what his grandfather said, and with his own mother's behavior years ago, and with the label. Three separate sources, same rule, no exceptions. Whatever the reason behind it, the adults in his life had a clear motive: keeping aspirin away from kids with flu or chickenpox, every time.

His fever came down that evening. He carried the acetaminophen and a glass of water back upstairs, and on the way he set the aspirin bottle, unopened, on the highest kitchen shelf where he couldn't reach it without a stool.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Most pencil cores are graphite powder mixed with clay, and adding more clay makes a harder pencil that leaves lighter marks.
story:
Scarlett sat at the kitchen table with a shoebox of pencils, a rubber eraser shaped like a strawberry, and a plan to draw a portrait of her cat, Biscuit, as a pirate. The problem was the shading. Her dark patches came out shiny and heavy, her light patches barely showed at all, and one pencil marked so faintly she wondered if it was haunted.

Kyson leaned over from the other side of the table, where he was supposed to be folding paper cranes but was mostly eating crackers. "That pencil's broken," he said. "Give it to me, I'll throw it out."

"It's not broken, it's mysterious." Scarlett held it up to the light like a detective. Then she remembered her grandmother's kitchen table, last summer, where she and Joel had sat drawing while the adults argued about crossword clues. Two yellow pencils, exactly the same size, and Joel's made fat dark storm clouds while hers made thin gray wisps. Joel had insisted his pencil was magic. Scarlett had insisted Joel was magic, which he enjoyed far too much. They'd never figured it out. "Grandma has a whole drawer of them," she said now, "and they're all different. It's like they're secretly different pencils wearing the same costume."

She lined up six pencils on the table and made a test strip, scribbling a small square with each one, darkest to lightest. The squares faded from black to ghost gray. On the sides of the pencils, when she squinted, she found tiny letters and numbers. 8B, 4B, HB, 2H, 4H.

"Those are pencil grades," Kyson said, mouth full. "My cousin tattoos them on her ankle." He was joking, but Scarlett wrote them down anyway. She noticed the ones with H made the palest marks, and she remembered Joel's magic cloud pencil had a B on it. B for bold, maybe. H for, what, humble?

Then she flipped a pencil fact card from her art kit, the one Ms. Aydın had handed out before winter break, expecting to cite it for a homework paragraph. Instead she found her answer right there: pencil cores are graphite powder mixed with clay, and adding more clay makes a harder pencil that leaves lighter marks. She read it twice, out loud, doing a news-anchor voice.

"So the clay ones are like an alloy," Kyson said. "Sort of. Mixed stuff."

"Sort of," Scarlett agreed, since arguing with Kyson was a waste of a good afternoon.

She tested it at once. The 4H, if it had more clay, should be hard and light. She pressed it hard into the paper and got only a whisper of gray, perfect for Biscuit's white ruffled shirt. The 8B went smudgy and dark, perfect for his eyepatch and his villainous eyebrows. The portrait came together so well that Kyson abandoned his cranes entirely and demanded a pirate crane in the corner.

"Fine," Scarlett said, "but it gets an eyepatch too."

"You're the best kind of strange," Kyson said, and held still for the strawberry eraser to be pressed ceremonially into his hand as payment.

activity: to use pivot tables in a spreadsheet to summarise survey answers by grade
knowledge_domain: to use pivot tables in a spreadsheet to summarise survey answers by grade
fact: A pivot table uses each column heading as a field name, so survey data needs one header row with a label at the top of every column.
story:
Jake had spent all of Tuesday's tech period collecting survey answers from sixth, seventh, and eighth graders about cafeteria food, and by Wednesday he had two hundred rows of data and no idea what any of it meant. Remy leaned over his shoulder in the computer lab.

"You could count by hand," Remy said.

"Two hundred rows. My hand would file a rebellion."

Ms. Wanjiru, walking past, tapped his screen. "A pivot table would summarize that in seconds. Try building one."

Jake clicked Insert, PivotTable, and a gray error box appeared: the command could not complete because the range contained a column with no heading. He stared at it, then at his sheet. Column A said Name, column B said Grade, and column C, where students had typed yes or no about liking the pizza, had nothing at the top. The first yes sat in the cell where a label should be.

"That's it," Jake said slowly. "Every column needs a label at the top. One header row. That's how the pivot table knows what the fields are called." He typed "Likes pizza" into C1, clicked Insert again, and this time the field list appeared like magic. He dragged Grade into Rows, Likes pizza into Columns, and counted into Values. Numbers sprang into a grid: how many sixth graders said yes, how many eighth graders said no, all of it tidy.

"It looks barren over there without you celebrating," said Devyn from the next computer. "Dance or something."

"I'm busy having a revelation," Jake said, though he did a small chair spin.

Then he noticed the twist. He had assumed eighth graders, being oldest and coolest, would deny liking cafeteria pizza. The table said the opposite: eighth grade had the highest yes count of all. "Wait. Look at this. Thirty-one eighth graders said yes and only nine said no." Devyn came over and squinted at the grid.

"Huh. I was sure they'd all pretend to hate it."

"Maybe that's just something we tell ourselves," Jake said. He copied the table into a chart and watched the sixth, seventh, and eighth grade bars orbit the pizza question like planets around a sun, every grade leaning the same way.

At the end of class Ms. Wanjiru asked how it went. Jake pointed at his screen, where the numbers were still glowing in their neat little squares. "Column C needed a name. Now it has one, and it's telling us everything."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Yeast makes bread rise by feeding on sugars and releasing carbon dioxide gas, which gets trapped in the dough as bubbles.
story:
Kate slammed the flour bag onto the counter and read the recipe card for the fourth time. "Tonight," she announced to the empty kitchen, "we are having real homemade bread, and nobody has to supervise me." Her dad had agreed to stay out of it, mostly, which meant he kept wandering past the door pretending to look for his keys.

She stirred warm water into a bowl, dumped in the yeast, and waited. Fifteen minutes later, the surface sat there, flat and indifferent, like a pond on a windless day. Nothing. No foam, no bubbles, nothing like the picture in the cookbook. Kate stared at it, then at the recipe, then back at the bowl. She had followed every step. Unless the yeast was dead, but the packet was brand new, and she had used half of it just last week for pizza dough that had worked fine.

She called Abbigail, who answered on the first ring because she was avoiding her math homework. "My dough is a brick," Kate said. "It won't rise. It's just sitting there."

"Did you check the water?" Abbigail asked. "Caelan killed his yeast last month. He used water straight from the kettle."

Kate held her hand under the kitchen tap and thought about it. She had run the water hot, because hot seemed better than cold for mixing. Too hot, maybe. But how could she know what too hot meant when she couldn't see anything happening to the yeast? Then she remembered her mom testing bath water for her little cousin, wrist first, water running over the inside of it. She tried it. The stream stung slightly against her skin, like a sunburn warming up. That was it. That was probably it.

She dumped the ruined bowl in the sink, rinsed it, and started over with water she could hold her wrist under comfortably. This time she watched the surface like it was a pot about to boil over. Five minutes. Eight. Then a thin cream-colored skin crept across the top, and underneath, tiny bubbles began stacking themselves up. "It's alive!" Kate shouted toward the living room. "Dad, it's foaming!"

She mixed the dough, kneaded it until her arms ached, and set it by the window with a towel over it. When Caelan biked over to see, the dough had climbed well above the bowl's rim, swollen and soft. "Yeast makes bread rise by feeding on sugars and releasing carbon dioxide gas," Kate told him, poking the dough and watching her fingertip print slowly spring back. "The gas gets trapped in the dough as bubbles. That's the whole trick." She cut one risen loaf open after baking, and the interior was full of holes, light and springy, exactly like bread from the bakery.

At dinner her dad tore off a chunk, buttered it, and went back for a second slice before he even said anything. Kate made a small pivot on her heel, arms crossed, grinning at the basket. "Next weekend," she said, "cinnamon rolls."

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: The United States Homestead Act of 1862 offered 160 acres of public land to settlers who lived on it and farmed it for five years.
story:
Maya pressed her notebook against the cold stone of the war memorial and squinted at the diary photocopy in her other hand. Ms. Bakker had brought the whole class out here because the old soldiers' names were carved into the granite, but Maya's assignment sat on the bench beside her: figure out, from one real document, why the Reed family had left Ohio for Kansas in 1871.

The diary was a primary source, the actual words of a settler named Harriet Reed, and Maya had read the same entry four times without it telling her anything. "The land here is poor and Father grows more discouraged each season," Harriet had written. "We hear talk of free land farther west, though the country there is arid and the rains uncertain." Maya wrote "arid" in her notes and underlined it twice, because dry land was something she could picture, even if she couldn't picture why anyone would run toward it.

"Why the long face?" Alizee dropped onto the bench and held out half of her granola bar, which Maya took, because it was cold out and Alizee always seemed to know that.

"The diary says they moved west for free land, but that can't be right. Land costs money. It's like the paper is hiding the reason, and I can't see it." Maya tapped the page. "Ms. Bakker says a primary source can be wrong, or missing things, so I have to check it."

That was when Leon came around the memorial's far side, waving his phone. "My grandpa found this in his mother's attic," he said, showing them a photograph of an old paper with faded ink. "It came with the diary stuff your teacher copied. Look." Maya read the heading aloud: "Homestead claim, 160 acres." Below it, in a clerk's careful hand, were the conditions. The United States Homestead Act of 1862 had offered 160 acres of public land to settlers who lived on it and farmed it for five years.

Maya sat very still, letting the two documents sit side by side in her mind. The diary said free land; the paper said how it became free. You had to stay five years and farm it. That was the hidden rule, and it explained everything, even why Harriet sounded worried all the time in later entries, since leaving early would cost them the whole farm. She looked up at the carved names on the memorial, soldiers from the same century, and felt the past click together like a puzzle she had been holding upside down.

"I want to test it," she said. "Harriet wrote again in 1876, if she stayed exactly five years, that should prove it. Can I simulate the timeline, just the dates, on graph paper?" Leon grinned and Alizee pulled a pencil from her bag and pressed it into Maya's hand.

Ms. Bakker leaned over Maya's shoulder a minute later and read the two dates Maya had circled, 1871 and 1876, with the words "160 acres, five years" between them. "Well," she said. "Can I borrow your pen? I want to draw an arrow from the claim paper to the diary, right here on your page."

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: Doctors warn against sliding objects like pencils or sticks into a cast to scratch an itch, because they can scrape the skin and damage the cast's lining.
story:
The itch started somewhere near Paige's left wrist, deep under the plaster where no finger could reach. She was buckled into the back seat of the family car, three hours into the drive to her grandmother's house, and the itch felt like a single industrious ant marching in slow circles.

"You're doing the face again," her dad said from the driver's seat, glancing at the mirror. "The grimace face."

"It's the itch," Paige said. "It moved. It was at my wrist before, and now it's halfway to my elbow. How does it even travel?" She reached down beside the seat, felt the metal edge of a ruler she kept there for science homework, and slid it out. The thin end fit perfectly into the gap at the wrist opening of her cast.

Her hand stopped in the air. Two weeks ago, in the doctor's office, the doctor had leaned close and said, "Do not slide anything in there. No pencils, no sticks, nothing like a ruler. Things like that can scrape the skin and wreck the lining of the cast." Paige remembered the word "lining," how the doctor tapped the hard shell like a knock on a door, as if something soft and important lived behind it.

She put the ruler down on the seat beside her. "I almost did a forbidden thing," she confessed out loud, mostly to the cast itself.

"What?" her dad asked.

"Nothing. Just talking to my arm." She flexed her fingers, wondering whether wiggling them might stir the air inside, like wind moving through a cave. It was worth testing. She wiggled slowly, then faster, and felt a faint coolness drift up along her skin. The itch paused, considered, then faded like a radio station driving out of range. She laughed. "It worked. Air. Just air."

Her phone buzzed. A text from Gloria: "did you try the ruler trick yet? Philip says a chopstick works even better, he did it when he broke his ankle."

Paige stared at the screen. Philip's cast had come off last month, and he had never mentioned a problem. But then, Philip was a little biased about his own ideas; he still claimed his volcano project should have won the science fair. She texted back: "doctor said it can scrape the skin and damage the cast's lining. don't do it. wiggle your fingers instead."

The phone buzzed again: "wait WHAT lining."

"inside the cast. go wiggle." Paige leaned her head against the window, watching fence posts flick past. Her wrist itched once more, faintly, like a question she had already answered. She wiggled her fingers, felt the small cool breeze travel up her arm, and smiled at the glass. "Best warranty on an itch," she murmured. "Fresh air, zero dollars."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Día de los Muertos, celebrated in Mexico mainly on November 1 and 2, honors family members who have died with home altars called ofrendas.
story:
Parker stood in the doorway of the community hall with a box of marigolds in his arms, following his mom toward the long tables at the far end. Ms. Ahmadi from the cultural center waved them over. "Perfect timing," she said. "We need meticulous hands for the petal path. One line of flowers from the door to the ofrenda, no gaps."

"The what?" Parker asked.

Olivia, who was already scattering petals, looked up. "The ofrenda. It's the altar." She pointed to the tiers at the head of the table, where candles, pan dulce, and little clay skulls waited to be arranged. "Día de los Muertos," she added. "It happens November first and second, and it's for people in your family who died."

Kurtis arrived with a stack of framed photos and set them down too hard, and one frame slid off the table. He caught it, but the backing popped loose, and a folded paper fell out. Parker picked it up. It was a letter, old and soft at the creases, written in looping cursive.

"Give it here," Olivia said, but Parker had already started reading, because the photo in the frame was a young man in a soldier's uniform, and the letter was addressed to him.

"Dear Tomas," Parker read under his breath. "The corn is in. Your mother saves the first tortilla for you every night, and she says you will find your way home by following the smell." He looked up. "Tomas is Olivia's great-grandfather, right? She said so when she brought the picture."

Ms. Ahmadi tilted her head toward the ofrenda. "Put the letter back where it belongs."

Parker didn't move. Something wasn't fitting. He looked at the petal path he was supposed to build, the unbroken line of orange from the door to the altar, and then at the letter in his hand. His mom had told him the petals were just decoration, but decoration didn't need to be one continuous line with no gaps. A path needed to go somewhere. And a letter that said "you will find your way home" needed a road.

"Ms. Ahmadi," he said slowly, "is the petal path for the people who died? So they can find the ofrenda?"

She smiled and said nothing, which was answer enough.

He knelt and laid the first marigold at the threshold, then worked backward toward the altar, checking each petal against the last, the way Kurtis was being meticulous about straightening the photo frames. Kurtis, meanwhile, had picked up the letter again, and his face had gone strange.

"Olivia," he said. "The signature. It's signed Papa. But Tomas was your great-grandfather. Your great-great-grandfather must have written it, and it was never sent." Kurtis held it out so they could both see. "It's dated the year after he died."

Olivia took the letter and stood very still, then placed it on the ofrenda beside the photo of the young soldier, smoothing the folds flat with two fingers.

"There," she said. "Now it arrived."

activity: to use pivot tables in a spreadsheet to summarise survey answers by grade
knowledge_domain: to use pivot tables in a spreadsheet to summarise survey answers by grade
fact: Putting the Grade field in a pivot table's Rows area lists each different grade once down the left side of the table.
story:
Alexis had a spreadsheet open on the kitchen laptop, 400 rows of survey answers stretching down the screen like a road with no end. She and Rae had spent a whole week collecting answers from students about the school cafeteria, promising everyone a report by Friday, and now all Alexis had was a shapeless pile of data. "How am I supposed to count these by hand?" she said to the empty room. Her dad suggested takeout as consolation, but she waved him off and kept staring.

Rae arrived after dinner with a bag of chips and zero ideas. "You could sort by grade," she offered, leaning over Alexis's shoulder. Alexis tried it, and it helped a little, but the list was still enormous, and every time she counted a section she lost her place. "There has to be a better way," Alexis muttered. "Mael said something about this once. He recruits half the school for his gaming club, so if anyone knows how to handle 400 people, it's him."

She texted Mael, and he called back from his uncle's porch, where he'd been helping string lights through the canopy of trees overhead. "Insert a pivot table," he said. "Drag the Grade field into Rows, then drag another field into Values. That's all I'll tell you, because I want to see if you can actually do it."

"It's not a battle, Mael."

"Everything's a little bit a battle."

Alexis clicked through the menu, half expecting disaster, and dropped Grade into the Rows area. The screen flickered and the whole wall of 400 answers collapsed into three neat rows running down the left side of the table: one for seventh grade, one for eighth, one for ninth. Each grade appeared exactly once, no matter how many hundreds of answers sat behind it. Rae grabbed her arm. "Wait, where did everything go?"

"Nowhere," Alexis said slowly, testing it. "It's all still there. The table just shows each different grade one time." She dragged the survey answer into Values, and counts bloomed beside each grade like she'd flipped a light on. Seventh grade, 152 answers. She sat back, grinning at the small tidy table that had swallowed a mountain.

Rae was already copying the numbers into their report. "This changes everything for Friday."

Alexis saved the file twice, then a third time to be sure. "Mael gets the first slice of whatever we're celebrating with."

"He'll demand synthetic cheese flavor," Rae said, snapping the chip bag shut.

activity: to improvise a blues solo over a twelve-bar chord progression
knowledge_domain: to improvise a blues solo over a twelve-bar chord progression
fact: Bending a guitar string pushes it sideways and stretches it tighter, which raises the note's pitch.
story:
Piper plugged her practice amp into the garage wall and set her feet on the cold concrete, guitar on her knee. The chord chart lay on an overturned milk crate beside her: twelve bars, the same loop over and over. Mr. García had told her to improvise a solo on top of it, and for three nights she had played nothing but safe notes that all sounded the same.

Oaklyn sat cross-legged on the old workbench, tapping the beat. Merrick had claimed a lawn chair and was spinning a drumstick like a tiny, versatile baton, which was his way of saying he was ready to keep time on the plastic buckets behind him. "Play something wild," Oaklyn said. "You're doing scales, not a solo."

"It's the blues," Piper said. "It's supposed to sound like something."

She thought about her grandfather's records, the way the guitar on them cried and bent and sagged. Those notes slid around, half of them not even real notes. She looped the progression again, and this time, on the fourth bar, she pushed the third string sideways with her finger, hard.

The note squealed, sharp and sour, like a rodent caught in a trap. Merrick winced. Oaklyn laughed so hard she nearly fell off the workbench. Piper froze, staring at her own finger. She had pressed the string sideways and it had stretched tighter across the fret, and the pitch had climbed way past where she wanted it. She tried again, gently, and the note rose just a little, a smooth little lift, like a voice asking a question instead of giving an answer. So that was the trick. She could control it, as long as she didn't oppose the string too hard.

"Again," Oaklyn said, and Piper looped the twelve bars once more. This time she bent on purpose, small on one bar, wider on the next, letting each note sag back down after it rose. Merrick dropped his drumstick and slapped a lazy shuffle on the buckets to match her. She hit one bend too far, sour again, but she let the sour note hang there on purpose, then slid down out of it, and somehow that sounded even bluer than the clean ones.

Her grandfather had quit piano lessons at twelve because a teacher told him he was playing it wrong, and Piper had never known whether to think that was brave or a waste. She decided she could worry about that later. The progression swung back around to bar one, and she leaned into the bend that had made her cry the first time she heard it on his old record, easing the string sideways until the note floated up and hung there, trembling, over Merrick's buckets.

"Right there," Oaklyn whispered. "Do that one again."

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Chinese culture, a clock is usually avoided as a gift, because the phrase 'giving a clock' sounds like a phrase about attending someone's death.
story:
Anais had one objective for Saturday: walk into the Wongs' housewarming with the perfect gift. She had been to their old apartment only once, for Mael's birthday, and she remembered how Mrs. Wong had pressed a second helping of noodles onto her plate before she'd finished the first, and how Mr. Wong had greeted her with both hands around his teacup, a small bow that made her feel suddenly very formal. The new house had a wide porch and a persimmon tree, and Anais wanted the gift to match.

At the shop she found a clock shaped like a bird, brass, with a soft tick she could hear from across the aisle. "Mael, look at this," she said, holding it up. "Their kitchen has that empty wall by the stove."

Mael went quiet in a way she had learned to diagnose like a change in weather. He set down the mug he'd been examining. "Get something else. Anything else."

"Why?"

He glanced toward the counter, then said it low and plain. "In Chinese culture, a clock is usually avoided as a gift, because the phrase 'giving a clock' sounds like a phrase about attending someone's death."

Anais put the bird clock down slowly, the way she'd seen people set down evidence in the courtroom shows she watched with her dad, like she was afraid the defendant would object. Her ears went hot. "You couldn't have mentioned this before I fell in love with it?"

"You fell in love with it ninety seconds ago." He picked up a lacquered tea tin and sniffed the jasmine through the lid. "This says the same thing. Welcome to your home, sit down, stay a while."

Anais tested the idea against what she remembered. Nobody in the Wong household had ever mentioned clocks, but there had been a moment at the birthday party when someone gave Mr. Wong a pocket knife and Mrs. Wong laughed and handed him a single coin in return, saying it made the knife a purchase, not a gift. So the family noticed things like this. Rules she couldn't see, but real ones. She bought the tea, plus a tin of almond cookies, and wrapped both in red paper because Mael said red was lucky.

At the gathering the steam from the dumplings fogged the kitchen window, and the little cousins were made to greet Anais with two hands around their juice cups like tiny ambassadors. When she presented her gift, Mrs. Wong held it in both palms and said, "So thoughtful, so thoughtful," and Anais felt her shoulders drop an inch.

Then Uncle Peter arrived, loudly, carrying a wrapped box with a bow. "For the new house!" he announced. "Everyone needs to know what time dinner is!"

It was a clock. A rooster, brass, ticking softly.

Mrs. Wong took it from him with both hands, smiling, and carried it straight to the empty wall by the stove, where she hung it and stepped back to admire it. "Perfect," she said. "We bought it for ourselves last week."

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A note's pitch depends on how fast the sound source vibrates: faster vibration makes a higher pitch, and slower vibration makes a lower one.
story:
Grandma's violin had been sitting on top of the wardrobe since at least last Thanksgiving, and Victoria had claimed it the moment she walked in the door. "You can keep it," Grandma had said, "if you can make it sound less like a duck in a dispute." That was the challenge, and Victoria intended to win it before Sunday dinner.

She tuned the A string carefully, bracing the scroll against the couch cushion so the old pegs would behave. Judah sprawled on the rug with his phone, offering expert commentary. "That sounds like a fire alarm with feelings," he said, and Victoria flicked his ankle with the bow. Alexa, cross-legged in the armchair, hummed the note back at her, then hummed it again a minute later, and Victoria noticed something odd. Alexa's hum had slid downward, and when she bowed the string again, hers had dropped too. The note was sinking on its own, slow as a melting ice cream cone.

Victoria refused to believe her playing was so bad the violin was losing the will to vibrate. She stared at the peg and formed a theory: the peg was loosening by itself, little by little. "So if the peg turns, the note changes," she said. "Tighter one way, looser the other. That's the pattern." To test it, she turned the peg a tiny amount in one direction and bowed. The pitch climbed higher, like a doorbell being stretched. She turned it back the other way and the note dropped low and grumpy. Faster vibration made the higher pitch; slower made the lower one, and the sneaky peg was choosing slow. "It's not me," she announced. "It's physics committing crimes."

They set up a stakeout. Alexa hummed the note every minute like a human thermostat, keeping the pitch stable, while Judah watched the peg and Victoria held the violin steady in the lamp light. When Alexa's hum slid down again, Judah shouted, "It moved! It's turning by itself!" The peg had crept backward a whisper. Victoria pushed it in snugly, and this time the note held, round and steady as a coin on a table.

At dinner, Grandma asked how the duck dispute was going. "The duck has been replaced by a swan," Victoria said, "though the swan occasionally squawks." Grandma laughed so hard she had to set down the mashed potatoes. After dinner, Victoria carried the violin back to the living room and played her three stable notes over and over, and Judah, who had given up mocking her, hummed along. "You know," he said, "that peg could symbolize every instrument that ever needed a good grip."
